agent.name: Embedded Project Idea Scoping Agent
agent.context: Embedded Engineering and Gen AI Summer School for third-year Computer Science students
agent.purpose: Convert a vague embedded project idea into a structured scoping brief for requirements engineering

fixed_platform.pin_policy: Use generic capabilities unless exact pins are provided
fixed_platform.logic_level_policy: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise

project.name: FRDM-MCXA153 Push-to-Talk Walkie Talkie Prototype
project.short_summary: A student prototype that uses the NXP FRDM-MCXA153 as the controller for a push-to-talk audio communication device, starting with local audio capture/playback indicators and scaling toward short-range digital voice exchange using an external 3.3 V-compatible communication module.
project.main_objective: Demonstrate the embedded-system building blocks of a walkie talkie: push-to-talk control, microphone input, speaker or headphone output, status feedback, and optional short-range wireless audio packet transfer.
project.operating_environment: Indoor lab or classroom prototype environment with short-range communication tests between two identical devices or between one device and a host-side simulator.
project.main_behavior: The user presses a push-to-talk control, speaks into a microphone, sees transmit status feedback, and releases the control to return to receive or idle mode. More advanced versions exchange compressed or low-rate audio over an external communication module.
inputs: Optional received wireless data from a paired unit
outputs: Speaker, buzzer, or headphone audio output
interaction_flow: Power the FRDM-MCXA153-based prototype from a verified supply.
Device starts in idle or receive mode and shows ready status.
User presses the push-to-talk button to enter transmit mode.
Firmware samples microphone audio or an audio module output and provides local status feedback.
Recommended version sends audio frames or voice activity events through an external communication module.
User releases the push-to-talk button and the device returns to receive or idle mode.
Received audio data, if implemented, is played back or represented through a speaker, headphone output, or diagnostic stream.
out_of_scope: Designing a regulated RF transmitter from discrete RF components
Guaranteed compatibility with commercial walkie talkies
Exact MCU pin assignment before board routing and peripheral configuration are reviewed

problem_space.purpose: Explore embedded audio, real-time interaction, and short-range communication through a recognizable push-to-talk device.
problem_space.physical_process_monitored_or_controlled: Human voice pressure waves are captured by a microphone, converted to an electrical or digital signal, optionally transmitted as data, and converted back to audible sound.
success_criteria: User can clearly control transmit and receive or idle states with a push-to-talk input.
Device provides visible feedback for ready, transmit, receive, and error states.
Core version demonstrates audio input and output locally or through diagnostics.
Recommended version demonstrates short-range voice or voice-like packet exchange between two prototypes or one prototype and a test receiver.
The prototype uses 3.3 V-compatible interfaces or includes clearly documented level shifting and power protection.
known_constraints: Exact pins and SDK APIs are not specified.
RF communication must use legal, pre-certified, or lab-approved modules rather than a custom radio transmitter.
Audio sampling, buffering, and playback timing need careful design even at low quality.
unknown_constraints: Whether two FRDM-MCXA153 boards are available.
Which microphone, speaker amplifier, and communication modules are available in the lab.
Permitted wireless frequency band and transmit power for the summer school setting.
Whether full voice audio, simple voice activity, or simulated packets are acceptable for the demonstration.

core_student_version.description: Build a single-board push-to-talk audio interface: button-controlled state machine, microphone level acquisition, simple audio output or tone feedback, LED status indicators, and serial debug logs.
expected_features: Microphone signal level capture using an ADC-capable input or digital audio module interface
Speaker, buzzer, or headphone output using a safe external driver if needed
LED status for idle, transmit, and error states
Serial debug output for sampled levels and state transitions
core_student_version.why_it_is_suitable: It teaches GPIO, timing, ADC or digital sensor input, output control, debugging, and state-machine design without depending on uncertain RF performance.

recommended_summer_school_version.description: Create a two-device short-range digital push-to-talk prototype using two FRDM-MCXA153 boards and a 3.3 V-compatible external communication module. The audio path may use low-rate sampled audio, encoded voice-like frames, or a simplified voice activity plus tone demonstration depending on available hardware.
expected_features: Two matching FRDM-MCXA153 prototypes or one prototype plus a host-side test peer
External 3.3 V-compatible communication module using a generic UART, SPI, or I2C-capable interface
Audio frame buffering with sequence numbers or timestamps
Receive status feedback and basic packet-loss indication
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_interesting: It turns a familiar consumer device into a concrete embedded systems challenge involving real-time behavior, communication protocols, and human interaction.
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_still_feasible: The RF complexity is delegated to an external module while students focus on firmware structure, buffering, user control, and testable communication behavior.

advanced_extension.description: Extend the prototype with better audio handling, packet diagnostics, optional storage, and GenAI-assisted development artifacts such as generated tests, protocol documentation, and debugging checklists.
advanced_features: Simple audio compression or voice activity detection
Ring buffers for transmit and receive audio frames
Packet loss, latency, and signal-quality logging
Small display for channel, mode, battery, and link status
Optional recording of short audio clips or diagnostics to external storage
Optional encryption or pairing concept for privacy discussion
PC-side visualization of audio level, packets, and state transitions
extra_components: External wireless module approved for lab use
Digital microphone or analog microphone breakout
Low-power speaker amplifier or headphone driver
Optional external flash or microSD module
Optional battery pack with proper regulation and protection
technical_challenges: Maintaining audio timing while handling user input and communication
Choosing a low enough audio rate for the available communication bandwidth
Managing half-duplex transmit and receive behavior
Keeping external module voltage, current, and logic levels compatible
risk_controls: Use pre-certified or lab-approved communication modules only.
Start with simulated or diagnostic audio frames before live voice.
Keep volume and amplifier power low for bench testing.
Document legal RF assumptions and require instructor approval before over-the-air tests.
Use generic pin capabilities until exact board configuration is confirmed.

main_board.name: NXP FRDM-MCXA153
main_board.reasoning: Mandatory board for all summer school projects

sensors.name: Microphone module
sensors.purpose: Capture voice or voice-level input for transmit mode.
sensors.likely_interface: ADC-capable input for analog microphone breakout, or generic digital audio-capable interface if a digital microphone module is selected
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: Prefer a 3.3 V-compatible module. Analog microphone boards may need biasing, gain, filtering, and careful signal-level verification.
risks: Raw microphone signal may be too small without an amplifier.
Some modules may expect 5 V or output levels unsuitable for direct MCU input.

actuators_outputs.name: Speaker, buzzer, or headphone output stage
actuators_outputs.purpose: Provide local tones, received audio playback, or diagnostics.
actuators_outputs.likely_interface: PWM-capable output, DAC-like filtered PWM approach, or external audio amplifier controlled through a generic output interface
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Do not drive a speaker directly from an MCU pin. Use a suitable low-power amplifier or buzzer driver and verify current limits.
risks: Speaker current can exceed MCU pin limits.
Audio amplifier modules may require power or logic levels that need verification.

actuators_outputs.name: Status LEDs
actuators_outputs.purpose: Show idle, transmit, receive, and error states.
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Use appropriate current-limiting resistors and board-safe drive levels.

user_inputs.name: Push-to-talk button
user_inputs.likely_interface: GPIO-capable pin with pull-up or pull-down configuration
user_inputs.notes: Debouncing should be handled in firmware or hardware.

user_inputs.name: Channel or mode buttons
user_inputs.purpose: Select channel, pairing ID, test mode, or volume mode.
user_inputs.notes: Optional for the recommended version; can be replaced by serial commands during early testing.

display_ui.name: Small status display
display_ui.purpose: Show channel, mode, link status, and diagnostics.
display_ui.notes: Optional; LEDs and serial output are enough for core and recommended prototypes.

communication_debug.name: USB serial debug connection
communication_debug.purpose: Log state changes, audio levels, packet counters, and errors.
communication_debug.likely_interface: USB interface or board debug serial interface
communication_debug.notes: Useful for bring-up and demonstration even if audio playback is limited.

communication_debug.name: External short-range communication module
communication_debug.purpose: Exchange voice frames or simplified audio packets between two devices.
communication_debug.likely_interface: Generic UART-capable, SPI-capable, or I2C-capable pins depending on selected module
communication_debug.notes: Choose a 3.3 V-compatible, legal, lab-approved module. Do not design a custom RF transmitter for this course project.

power_source.recommended_power: Use the board's normal development power path for bench testing. Add external regulated power only if audio amplifier, radio module, or battery operation requires it.
power_source.notes: Battery operation is optional and should use a protected battery pack or regulated supply approved by instructors.
risks: Audio amplifiers and wireless modules may draw more current than the board can safely provide.
Incorrect battery wiring or unregulated supplies can damage the board.

optional_advanced_components.name: Pre-certified wireless module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Provide the actual radio link without custom RF design.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Makes the walkie talkie concept demonstrable while keeping RF hardware realistic.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Availability, bandwidth, legal limitations, or driver complexity may exceed the course schedule.
risks: Module may not support enough bandwidth for raw audio.
Module may require level shifting, external antenna rules, or specific regulatory limits.

optional_advanced_components.name: External flash or microSD module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Store audio clips, logs, or packet traces.
risks: Storage writes may interfere with real-time audio timing.
Some modules may be 5 V-oriented and require verification.

optional_advanced_components.name: Battery pack with regulator and protection
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Power safety and charging circuitry can distract from the embedded communication objective.
risks: Battery safety risk if unprotected cells or incorrect charging are used.
Voltage drops can reset the board during audio or radio peaks.

software_context.recommended_development_environment: NXP-supported FRDM-MCXA153 development workflow selected by the course staff, using board examples for GPIO, timers, serial debug, and the selected audio or communication interfaces.
recommended_sdk_or_libraries: Board support package and examples for FRDM-MCXA153
UART, SPI, or I2C examples matching the selected communication module
Optional lightweight ring-buffer or packet protocol helper code written by students
software_context.suggested_starting_point: Start from a minimal FRDM-MCXA153 project that blinks LEDs and prints serial debug logs, then add push-to-talk input, microphone sampling or audio-level reading, local output, and finally the selected communication module.
debugging_interfaces: Optional logic analyzer for timing and communication signals
Optional host-side script for packet inspection

constraints.voltage: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise
constraints.power: External audio and radio components must have verified current requirements and should not be powered from MCU pins.
constraints.timing: Audio capture, playback, and packet transfer require bounded timing, buffering, and clear half-duplex state transitions.
constraints.memory: Raw audio buffers can consume memory quickly, so low sample rates, short frames, and bounded ring buffers are recommended.
constraints.safety: Avoid high volume, unsafe batteries, direct speaker drive from MCU pins, and unapproved RF transmission.
constraints.privacy_security: Voice communication may capture personal speech; demonstrations should avoid sensitive content and should document whether transmissions are open or paired.

complexity.reason: The idea is attractive and teachable, but real-time voice communication and RF constraints can become difficult. A staged design keeps the core achievable while leaving full digital voice exchange as a recommended or advanced goal.

facts_provided_by_user: Project must use the NXP FRDM-MCXA153 board
A core student version, recommended version, and advanced extension are required
Exact pins and SDK APIs must not be invented

assumptions.assumption: The project is intended as an educational prototype, not a certified consumer radio product.
assumptions.reason: The input is a broad concept and the summer school context favors learning outcomes over product certification.

assumptions.assumption: A pre-certified or lab-approved external communication module will be used for any over-the-air wireless link.
assumptions.reason: Custom RF transmitter design is not appropriate for a short student embedded project and may raise legal constraints.

assumptions.assumption: The recommended version may use reduced audio quality, simplified voice frames, or a host-side peer if two complete boards are not available.
assumptions.reason: This keeps the demonstration feasible despite unknown module bandwidth and hardware availability.

assumptions.assumption: All external modules will be checked for 3.3 V logic compatibility before connection to the FRDM-MCXA153.
assumptions.reason: The brief must not assume 5 V compatibility or safe direct connection.

open_questions.question: Should the demonstration require real voice audio between two devices, or is a staged prototype with audio levels, tones, and packet diagnostics acceptable?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This determines audio bandwidth, buffer size, module choice, and schedule risk.

open_questions.question: Which microphone, speaker amplifier, and wireless modules are available to students?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Hardware availability drives interface choice, power design, and achievable audio quality.

open_questions.question: Are two FRDM-MCXA153 boards available per project team?
open_questions.why_it_matters: A two-device walkie talkie is the most natural demonstration, but a host-side peer can reduce hardware needs.

open_questions.question: What wireless bands, transmit powers, and lab policies are approved for student use?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Over-the-air communication must remain legal and safe.

open_questions.question: Is portable battery operation required or only optional?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Battery operation adds power, safety, enclosure, and testing complexity.

technical: Audio capture and playback may require more timing precision than expected.
Communication module bandwidth may be insufficient for raw audio.
Two-way behavior must be half-duplex to avoid complex mixing and collision handling.
Debugging audio quality can be difficult without instrumentation.
safety: Speaker or headphone output should be kept at safe volume levels.
Battery-powered operation requires protected cells and correct regulation.
No safety-critical or emergency communication claims should be made.
voltage_power: External audio amplifiers and wireless modules may require more current than available from board headers.
Some common breakout boards are designed for 5 V operation or have unclear logic levels.
Directly driving a speaker from an MCU pin can damage the board.
timing: Audio sampling, packet transmission, and playback can conflict without buffering.
Button debounce and mode switching must not disrupt audio frames.
Storage or display updates in the advanced version can introduce latency.
memory: Unbounded audio buffers can exceed MCU RAM.
Diagnostics and optional logging must use fixed-size buffers or controlled sampling.
privacy_security: Voice transmission can expose personal speech.
Unencrypted wireless links may be observable by nearby receivers depending on module and protocol.
Pairing, channel selection, or device IDs should be documented to avoid accidental cross-talk.
advanced_feature_risks: Audio compression and voice activity detection may consume significant CPU time.
Battery portability and enclosure work can distract from firmware learning goals.
Adding display, storage, and wireless simultaneously can exceed the summer school schedule.

human_approval_required: Approve the selected scope: core, recommended, or advanced.
Approve the wireless module and confirm it is legal and lab-approved.
Approve external microphone and speaker amplifier modules after voltage and current checks.
Approve whether real voice exchange is required for the final demonstration.

handoff_to_requirements_agent.readiness_notes: The project is ready for requirements engineering if the requirements agent treats the recommended scope as a staged push-to-talk digital audio prototype and keeps exact pins, SDK calls, wireless module choice, and audio quality as decisions to confirm.
critical_missing_information: Number of FRDM-MCXA153 boards per team
Approved wireless policy for the lab
Required audio fidelity and final demonstration expectations
